title: Height Checker
description: Count how many positions differ between the current array and its sorted version, using counting sort for the comparison.

blocks.text: Students stand in a line with heights given by heights. If the students were instead sorted by height, some students would end up in different positions. Return the number of indices where the current heights array differs from what it would be if sorted in non-decreasing order.

blocks.caption: Comparing the array against a sorted copy, position by position, counts the out-of-place entries.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","heights[] (current order)"],["Comparison","Against heights sorted in non-decreasing order"],["Output","Count of indices where the two differ"]]}

blocks.text: "How many positions differ from the sorted version" is directly answered by comparing the array to a sorted copy of itself, position by position. Since heights are bounded small integers (typically up to 100 in this problem's constraints), a counting sort can build that sorted copy without an O(n log n) comparison sort.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Counting sort is a good fit whenever values are known to fall within a small, bounded range, turning an O(n log n) sort into an O(n + range) one.

Picture a lineup of students by their current arrangement, and a second, ideal lineup sorted by height. At each position, if the student differs between the two lineups, that position counts as "out of place." The answer is simply how many positions are out of place.

blocks.caption: Comparing the current lineup to the height-sorted lineup, position by position.

items: Build the sorted (expected) version of heights.
Compare heights[i] to expected[i] for every index i.
Count how many indices have a mismatch.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: There are 3 mismatched indices (2, 4, and 5), matching the expected output of 3.
Building the expected array with a general-purpose comparison sort works and is simple, costing O(n log n).

Since heights fall within a small known range (a common constraint for this specific problem), a counting sort builds the sorted expected array in O(n + range) by counting occurrences of each height value, then reconstructing the sorted order by walking through the possible values in increasing order and emitting each the number of times it occurred.
Sort a copy of heights with a general comparison sort, then count mismatches against the original array.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: This is already an efficient and simple solution; the counting sort below trades the log n factor for a dependency on the value range, useful specifically because heights are known to be small bounded integers here.

Count how many times each height value appears. Then walk through possible height values in increasing order, emitting each value as many times as it occurred, comparing each emitted value against the original array's next position, counting mismatches along the way. This builds and compares against the sorted order without an explicit comparison sort.

items: Count occurrences of each height value into a counts array, sized to the maximum height plus one.
Walk values from 0 to maxHeight; for each value, emit it counts[value] times, comparing to heights[idx] and advancing idx each time.
Increment the mismatch count whenever the emitted expected value differs from the original.

Counting sort avoids the log n factor of a comparison sort whenever the value range is small and known in advance.
This exact pattern, count occurrences then reconstruct sorted order by walking the value range, reapplies to any problem needing a sorted array of small-range integers.

blocks.text: Height Checker is solved by building the height-sorted expected array (via counting sort, since heights are small bounded integers) and comparing it position by position against the original array, counting mismatches in O(n + range) time.
